citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be an
invertible linear map ([[def-linear-map]]). Then:

1. $T[E]$ is a Borel set for every Borel set $E$, and $T$ carries open sets to
   open sets;
2. there is a strictly positive real $c(T)$, namely
   $c(T) = \lambda_n\big(T[(0,1]^n]\big)$, with
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; c(T)\,\lambda_n(E) \qquad \text{for every } E \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n);$$
3. $c(S \circ T) = c(S)\,c(T)$ for invertible linear $S$ and $T$, and
   $c(\mathrm{id}) = 1$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim:
Choose $x_0\in\operatorname{int}W$ and $r>0$ with the open ball $B(x_0,r)\subseteq W$. For $0<t<1$ put $W_t=x_0+(1-t)(W-x_0)$. If $w\in W$ and $\|z\|<tr$, then $x_0+z/t\in B(x_0,r)\subseteq W$ and
$$(1-t)w+t(x_0+z/t)=(1-t)w+tx_0+z\in W$$
by convexity; thus every point of $W_t$ has an open ball of radius $tr$ contained in $W$, so $W_t\subseteq\operatorname{int}W$.

If $0<t'<t<1$, put $w'=\frac{1-t}{1-t'}w+\frac{t-t'}{1-t'}x_0$. The two coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one, so $w'\in W$ by convexity, and
$$x_0+(1-t)(w-x_0)=x_0+(1-t')(w'-x_0).$$
Thus $W_t\subseteq W_{t'}$. Moreover, every $y\in\operatorname{int}W$ lies in some $W_t$: for $y\ne x_0$, choose $s>0$ small enough that $w=x_0+(1+s)(y-x_0)\in W$, and then $y=x_0+(1-t)(w-x_0)$ for $t=s/(1+s)$; $x_0$ lies in every $W_t$. Hence for any sequence $t_n\downarrow0$, $W_{t_n}\uparrow\operatorname{int}W$.

By [F2] and [F3], $|W_{t_n}|=(1-t_n)^d|W|$ and the sets increase to $\operatorname{int}W$, so [F3] gives $|\operatorname{int}W|=|W|$. Thus the compact boundary $\partial W=W\setminus\operatorname{int}W$ is a null set. Since $W$ contains a nonempty open ball and is bounded, [F1] gives $0<|W|<\infty$.

Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $t>0$ so that $|W|-|W_t|=(1-(1-t)^d)|W|<\epsilon$. Choose a grid of half-open cubes of side $\delta< tr/\sqrt d$. Each cube that intersects $W_t$ is contained in $W$, because its points lie within distance at most $\sqrt d\delta<tr$ of a point whose radius-$tr$ ball lies in $W$. Only finitely many grid cubes intersect bounded $W_t$; their union $R$ is disjoint, finite, contains $W_t$, and is contained in $W$. Therefore $|W\setminus R|\le |W\setminus W_t|<\epsilon$.

Fix $\epsilon>0$ and choose $R\subseteq W$ as in step 2.2, a finite union of disjoint rectangles. Translation invariance and the symmetric-difference inclusion give
$$|(W+h)\triangle W|\le2|W\setminus R|+|(R+h)\triangle R|.$$
For each half-open rectangle, its overlap with a translate by $h$ has volume tending to the rectangle's volume as $h\to0$, by the box-volume formula; the same limit holds for their finite union. Thus $\limsup_{h\to0}|(W+h)\triangle W|\le2\epsilon$, and arbitrariness of $\epsilon$ gives convergence to zero.
For $a>0$, [F2] gives $|aW|=a^d|W|$ and $|(aW+x)\triangle aW|=a^d|(W+x/a)\triangle W|$. Dividing and applying step 3.1 with $h=x/a\to0$ proves the asserted boundary ratio.

Steps 2.1–3.2 prove positive finite volume, the finite inner rectangle approximation, dilation scaling, and the translated-boundary limit. Countable Choice is used only through [F1]–[F2]; no AC or DC is used.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes nonempty interior, so an empty or lower-dimensional W is outside the theorem; the inscribed-ball construction in step 1.1 uses that hypothesis.
Step 2.1 shows 0<|W|<∞ from an inscribed ball and boundedness, so zero volume is excluded by the stated nonempty-interior hypothesis.
The proof applies to d≥1 and the one-dimensional interval case is covered by the same convex homothety and grid arguments in steps 1.1–3.2.
A compact convex set with empty interior is explicitly excluded; step 1.1 requires an interior ball.
The approximation uses disjoint half-open grid cubes and the translated-boundary limit in steps 2.2–3.2, so cube boundaries follow the stated convention.
Countable Choice is declared in A1 and used only through the measure suppliers, as recorded in step 4.1.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process supplier. Let $\eta$ be a Poisson point process on $\mathbb R^d$ with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure $\nu$. For every nonnegative function $h$ measurable on the product of the Borel and configuration evaluation sigma-algebras,

$$\mathbb E\int h(x,\eta-\delta_x)\,\eta(dx)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbb E[h(x,\eta)]\,\nu(dx).$$

At each counted occurrence $x$, $\eta-\delta_x$ removes exactly one occurrence; coincident remaining occurrences stay. Equivalently, for every such nonnegative $f$,

$$\mathbb E\int f(x,\eta)\,\eta(dx)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbb E[f(x,\eta+\delta_x)]\,\nu(dx).$$

Both sides are extended nonnegative integrals.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process supplier. For every stationary locally finite point process $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite positive intensity $\rho$, there is a unique probability law $P^0$ on the configuration space satisfying

$$\mathbb E\int h(x,\theta_x\eta)\,\eta(dx)=\rho\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int h(x,\mu)\,P^0(d\mu)\,dx$$

for every nonnegative product-measurable $h$. Moreover, $P^0$-almost every configuration has at least one occurrence at the origin.

Let $\mu$ be a locally finite counting measure as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, its **recentering at $x$** is the counting measure $\theta_x\mu$ defined on Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ by

$$(\theta_x\mu)(B):=\mu(B+x).$$

Thus an occurrence at $x$ is moved to $0$, and in an occurrence representation $\mu=\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$ one has $\theta_x\mu=\sum_i\delta_{X_i-x}$. The action obeys $\theta_{x+y}=\theta_x\circ\theta_y$ and $\theta_0$ is the identity. Joint measurability in $(x,\mu)$ is proved in [[lem-joint-measurability-of-spatial-recentering]].

**Axiom convention.** The point-process supplier used for this definition has transitive dependencies on AC and Countable Choice; the recentering formula itself makes no selections.
The map $(x,\mu)\mapsto\theta_x\mu$ from $\mathbb R^d$ times the evaluation-measurable space of locally finite counting measures to that space is measurable.

Assume AC and Countable Choice, as carried by the random-point-process supplier. Let $\eta$ be a stationary locally finite point process on $\mathbb R^d$ with $0<\rho:=\mathbb E[\eta(Q)]<\infty$, where $Q=[0,1)^d$. Its mean measure $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$ is

$$\nu(B)=\rho\lambda_d(B)$$

for every Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process and Palm suppliers. Let $\eta$ be stationary and locally square integrable as in [[def-stationary-point-process-and-intensity]] and [[def-second-factorial-and-reduced-moment-measures]], with finite positive intensity $\rho$ and reduced second factorial moment measure $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$.

A **pair-correlation density** exists exactly when $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Borel Lebesgue measure [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Local finiteness makes $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ sigma-finite, so [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives a density; positivity of the measure makes that density nonnegative almost everywhere, and replacing its values on the null exceptional set by zero gives a nonnegative Borel version. The density is unique up to Lebesgue-null sets. Normalize it by $\rho^2$ and call the resulting nonnegative Borel function $g$:

$$\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D)=\rho^2\int_D g(u)\,du$$

for every Borel $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. The definition does not assume pair densities for all stationary processes.

For $r\ge0$, let $B[0,r]=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2\le r\}$ be the **closed** Euclidean ball. **Ripley's K-function** is

$$K(r):=\rho^{-1}\int(\mu-\delta_0)(B[0,r])\,P^0(d\mu),$$

where $P^0$ is the full Palm distribution from [[def-full-palm-distribution]] and $\delta_0$ removes one distinguished occurrence at the origin. The Palm law has an origin occurrence almost surely by [[thm-refined-campbell-formula-and-palm-law-existence]], and the reduced-measure identity [[thm-reduced-second-factorial-moment-palm-identity]] gives the equivalent expression $K(r)=\rho^{-2}\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(B[0,r])$. For a simple process as defined in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]], deleting $\delta_0$ is the same as excluding the origin location; for a multiplicity-bearing process other co-located occurrences remain.

**Axiom convention.** AC and Countable Choice are inherited through the point-process and Palm dependency closure; no further choice is used by these definitions.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Let $S$ be as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. A
**Poisson point process with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure
$\nu$** is a point process $\eta$ such that for every finite pairwise-disjoint
family of Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_m$, the counts $\eta(B_i)$ are independent
random elements ([[def-independent-random-elements]]) and $\eta(B_i)$ has the
scalar Poisson law of mean $\nu(B_i)$
([[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]],
[[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]). If $\nu(B)=\infty$,
the extended count convention is $\eta(B)=+\infty$ almost surely.
Here sigma-finite means that $S$ is a countable union of Borel sets of finite
$\nu$-measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]); for the
stated $S$, local finiteness also implies sigma-finiteness by the compact
exhaustion in
[[lem-locally-compact-second-countable-spaces-have-compact-exhaustions]].

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the evaluation-measurable space of locally
finite Borel measures. A **Cox point process directed by a random measure
$\xi$** consists of a point process $\eta$, a random locally finite measure
$\xi$, and a supplied probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$
to $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ such that $K(\xi,\cdot)$ is a regular
conditional law of $\eta$ given $\xi$
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]) and, for $P_\xi$-almost every
$\mu$, $K(\mu,\cdot)$ is the law of a Poisson point process of intensity
$\mu$. The kernel is part of the model data; this definition does not assert
that such a kernel exists for every $(\eta,\xi)$. The mean measure of $\xi$ is
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, a measure by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]].

Both definitions permit multiplicities. They do not assert that diffuse
directing measures yield simple processes or that a Cox law determines the law
of its directing measure.

derivations.claim: For each compact $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, [F6] gives $\mathbb E[\eta(C)^2]=(\rho|C|)^2+\rho|C|<\infty$, so $\eta$ is locally square integrable and satisfies the second-order premise of the K definition [F5].

Fix a configuration event $A$. In [F1] use
$$h_A(x,\mu)=\mathbf1_Q(x)\mathbf1_A(\theta_x(\mu+\delta_x)),$$
which is product measurable by [F3] and the evaluation formula for adding one atom. At each occurrence $x$ of $\eta$, deletion followed by addition restores $\eta$, so the left side is $\mathbb E\int\mathbf1_Q(x)\mathbf1_A(\theta_x\eta)\eta(dx)$.

The right side of that Mecke identity is
$$\rho\int_Q\mathbb P(\theta_x(\eta+\delta_x)\in A)\,dx=\rho|Q|\mathbb P(\eta+\delta_0\in A),$$
because $\theta_x\delta_x=\delta_0$ and stationarity gives $\theta_x\eta\stackrel d=\eta$. The refined Palm identity [F2] applied to $\mathbf1_Q(x)\mathbf1_A(\mu)$ says that the left side in step 1.2 is $\rho|Q|P^0(A)$. Since $|Q|=1$ and $\rho>0$, $P^0(A)=\mathbb P(\eta+\delta_0\in A)$ for every $A$, proving the full-Palm law identity.

Under this Palm law, $\mu$ has the distribution of $\eta+\delta_0$. Removing the single distinguished occurrence gives $(\eta+\delta_0)-\delta_0=\eta$ even if $\eta$ has other occurrences at $0$. Therefore
$$\mathbb E^0[(\mu-\delta_0)(B[0,r])]=\mathbb E[\eta(B[0,r])]=\rho|B[0,r]|$$
by [F4]. Substituting in the K definition [F5] yields $K(r)=|B[0,r]|$.

The endpoint $r=0$ is included: the closed ball is $\{0\}$ and the same calculation gives $K(0)=\rho^{-1}\mathbb E\eta(\{0\})=0=|\{0\}|$. The proof uses the one-occurrence deletion convention and asserts neither diffuse-intensity simplicity nor any other simplicity property. AC and Countable Choice [A1]–[A2] are inherited supplier assumptions.

boundaries.evidence: For r=0 the closed ball is {0}; step 3.1 verifies K(0)=0.

Fix a locally compact, second-countable Hausdorff topological space $S$
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-second-countable-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Here locally compact means that every point has a
compact neighbourhood; second countable means that the topology has an at most
countable basis; and Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint open
neighbourhoods. Let $\mathcal B(S)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the
open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A **counting measure** on $S$ is a Borel measure of the form
$\mu=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{x_j}$ for a finite or countable index set $J$ and
points $x_j\in S$, where repetitions are allowed and the empty sum is zero.
Each $\delta_x$ is the unit point mass at $x$
([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), and
the countable sum is a measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]. The **multiplicity** at $x$ is
$\mu(\{x\})$. The counting measure is **locally finite** if
$\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact subset $K\subseteq S$
([[def-compact-space]]).

Let $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of locally finite counting
measures, equipped with the sigma-algebra generated by the **evaluation maps**
$\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(S)$. A **point process** on $S$ is a
measurable map $\eta:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to
(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$ from a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), with measurability in the sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Equivalently, every
count $\eta(B)$ is a measurable random variable, because the evaluation maps
generate $\mathcal E$. Its **law** is the probability measure
$\mathbb P_\eta(A)=\mathbb P(\eta^{-1}(A))$ on $(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]],
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]). The process is
classified by its realized configurations: a configuration $\mu$ is
**simple** if $\mu(\{x\})\le1$ for every $x$, and is **multiplicity-bearing**
if some singleton has mass greater than one. This is a pointwise distinction;
no almost-sure simplicity assertion is part of this definition.

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of all locally finite Borel
measures on $S$, with the sigma-algebra generated by their evaluation maps. A
**random locally finite measure** $\xi$ is a measurable map into this space.

For a nonnegative Borel function $f$, write
$\eta(f):=\int_S f\,d\eta$. Define the expected measure, or **intensity
measure**, by $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$. The expected-measure and
random-integral measurability assertions are justified by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]]. The measure
$\nu$ need not be locally finite; it is locally finite exactly when
$\mathbb E[\eta(K)]<\infty$ for each compact $K$.

The mean measure of a random locally finite measure is likewise
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, covered by the same expected-measure lemma. Local
finiteness of each realization does not by itself assert local finiteness of
$\nu$.

Work with a point process $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and its law $P_\eta$ on the evaluation-measurable configuration space from [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. Recentering $\theta_x$ is as in [[def-spatial-recentering-action]]. The process is **stationary** if $\theta_x\eta$ has law $P_\eta$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$.

Put $Q=[0,1)^d$. Its **intensity** is $\rho:=\mathbb E[\eta(Q)]$. It has **finite positive intensity** when $0<\rho<\infty$. The item [[thm-stationary-point-process-intensity-measure-is-rho-lebesgue]] proves that its mean measure is $\rho\lambda_d$ under the stated measure-theoretic assumptions.

The **translation-invariant sigma-algebra** is
$$\mathcal I_\eta:=\{A\text{ in the configuration sigma-algebra}: P_\eta(\theta_x^{-1}A\mathbin{\triangle}A)=0\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb R^d\}.$$
It is a sigma-algebra because symmetric-difference nullity is preserved by complements and countable unions. The stationary point process is **ergodic under translations** if every $A\in\mathcal I_\eta$ has $P_\eta(A)\in\{0,1\}$. This is the full $\mathbb R^d$ action convention, not ergodicity of one selected unit shift.

**Axiom convention.** This item carries AC and Countable Choice through the transitive well-definedness dependencies of the point-process supplier; stationarity and the scalar intensity definition themselves use no choices.

Let $\mu$ be a locally finite counting measure as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, its **recentering at $x$** is the counting measure $\theta_x\mu$ defined on Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ by

$$(\theta_x\mu)(B):=\mu(B+x).$$

Thus an occurrence at $x$ is moved to $0$, and in an occurrence representation $\mu=\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$ one has $\theta_x\mu=\sum_i\delta_{X_i-x}$. The action obeys $\theta_{x+y}=\theta_x\circ\theta_y$ and $\theta_0$ is the identity. Joint measurability in $(x,\mu)$ is proved in [[lem-joint-measurability-of-spatial-recentering]].

**Axiom convention.** The point-process supplier used for this definition has transitive dependencies on AC and Countable Choice; the recentering formula itself makes no selections.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process supplier. For every stationary locally finite point process $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite positive intensity $\rho$, there is a unique probability law $P^0$ on the configuration space satisfying

$$\mathbb E\int h(x,\theta_x\eta)\,\eta(dx)=\rho\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int h(x,\mu)\,P^0(d\mu)\,dx$$

for every nonnegative product-measurable $h$. Moreover, $P^0$-almost every configuration has at least one occurrence at the origin.

Assume $\eta$ is a stationary point process as in [[def-stationary-point-process-and-intensity]]. It is **locally square integrable** if $\mathbb E[\eta(K)^2]<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. For a realized counting measure $\mu=\sum_{i\in J}\delta_{X_i}$, with occurrences indexed separately even when locations coincide, as allowed by [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]], define its second factorial measure on Borel $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ by

$$\mu^{(2)}(C):=\sum_{i,j\in J,\ i\ne j}\mathbf1_C(X_i,X_j).$$

The **second factorial moment measure** is $\alpha^{(2)}(C):=\mathbb E[\eta^{(2)}(C)]$. With $Q=[0,1)^d$, the **reduced second factorial moment measure** is

$$\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D):=\mathbb E\sum_{i,j\in J,\ i\ne j}\mathbf1_Q(X_i)\mathbf1_D(X_j-X_i),\qquad D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ Borel}.$$

The local theorem [[thm-second-factorial-and-reduced-measures-are-locally-finite]] proves measurability and local finiteness under local square integrability. Occurrence indices, rather than distinct locations, are essential when multiplicities are present.

**Axiom convention.** AC and Countable Choice are carried by the transitive point-process supplier dependencies; the occurrence-indexed formulas themselves make no selections.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process and Palm suppliers. Let $\eta$ be stationary and locally square integrable as in [[def-stationary-point-process-and-intensity]] and [[def-second-factorial-and-reduced-moment-measures]], with finite positive intensity $\rho$ and reduced second factorial moment measure $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$.

A **pair-correlation density** exists exactly when $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Borel Lebesgue measure [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Local finiteness makes $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ sigma-finite, so [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives a density; positivity of the measure makes that density nonnegative almost everywhere, and replacing its values on the null exceptional set by zero gives a nonnegative Borel version. The density is unique up to Lebesgue-null sets. Normalize it by $\rho^2$ and call the resulting nonnegative Borel function $g$:

$$\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D)=\rho^2\int_D g(u)\,du$$

for every Borel $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. The definition does not assume pair densities for all stationary processes.

For $r\ge0$, let $B[0,r]=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2\le r\}$ be the **closed** Euclidean ball. **Ripley's K-function** is

$$K(r):=\rho^{-1}\int(\mu-\delta_0)(B[0,r])\,P^0(d\mu),$$

where $P^0$ is the full Palm distribution from [[def-full-palm-distribution]] and $\delta_0$ removes one distinguished occurrence at the origin. The Palm law has an origin occurrence almost surely by [[thm-refined-campbell-formula-and-palm-law-existence]], and the reduced-measure identity [[thm-reduced-second-factorial-moment-palm-identity]] gives the equivalent expression $K(r)=\rho^{-2}\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(B[0,r])$. For a simple process as defined in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]], deleting $\delta_0$ is the same as excluding the origin location; for a multiplicity-bearing process other co-located occurrences remain.

**Axiom convention.** AC and Countable Choice are inherited through the point-process and Palm dependency closure; no further choice is used by these definitions.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process and Palm suppliers. Let $\eta$ be a stationary locally square-integrable point process on $\mathbb R^d$ with intensity $0<\rho<\infty$, let $P^0$ be its full Palm distribution, and let $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}$ use $Q=[0,1)^d$. For every Borel $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D)=\rho\int (\mu-\delta_0)(D)\,P^0(d\mu).$$

The subtraction removes one distinguished occurrence at the origin; any other co-located occurrences remain.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For every Borel $B$, $u\mapsto\eta_u(B)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mathbf1_B(k+u)$ is measurable as a countable sum of Borel functions; every compact set meets only finitely many points of each $\eta_u$, so this is a locally finite random counting measure. For fixed $x$, put $t=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in[0,1)$. The map $u\mapsto\{u-x\}$ is a translation on each of $[0,t)$ and $[t,1)$, with the two image intervals partitioning $[0,1)$; by [F2] it preserves uniform probability. Reindexing $k\in\mathbb Z$ gives $\theta_x\eta_u=\eta_{\{u-x\}}$, so the process is stationary. Since exactly one $k+u$ lies in $Q=[0,1)$ for every $u\in[0,1)$, $\eta_U(Q)=1$ and $\rho=1$.

For every compact $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, choose an integer $m\ge1$ with $C\subseteq[-m,m]$. If $u\in[0,1)$ and $k+u\in C$, then $-m-1\le k\le m$, so $\eta_u(C)\le2m+2$ uniformly in $u$. Consequently $\mathbb E[\eta_U(C)^2]\le(2m+2)^2<\infty$ and $\mathbb E[(2\eta_U)(C)^2]\le4(2m+2)^2<\infty$. Both lattice processes satisfy the local square-integrability premise in the second-order and K definitions.

For every configuration event $A$, the unit-cube Palm construction in [F3] gives
$$P^0(A)=\mathbb E\int_Q\mathbf1_A(\theta_x\eta_U)\eta_U(dx).$$
There is exactly one occurrence $x=U$ in $Q$, and $\theta_U\eta_U=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\delta_k=:\Lambda$. Therefore $P^0=\delta_\Lambda$. In particular, using the uncentered configuration in the indicator $\mathbf1_{\{\mu(\{0\})>0\}}$ would give $0$ on the left Campbell sum almost surely, whereas the Palm-side value is $1$; this is why recentering cannot be dropped.

For each selected lattice occurrence $X_i=k+U\in Q$, the displacements to all other occurrences are $\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$. Hence [F4] gives $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D)=\#(D\cap(\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}))$ for bounded Borel $D$. In particular $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(\{1\})=1$ while $|\{1\}|=0$, so no measurable density $g$ can satisfy [F5].

Now put $\widetilde\eta_U=2\eta_U$, so every lattice site has two occurrence indices and $\widetilde\rho=2$. A selected occurrence has one other occurrence at the same site, so $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(\{0\})=2$. Equivalently, $P^0$ is concentrated on $2\Lambda$, and $\mu(\{0\})=2$, so [F6] gives $2=\widetilde\rho\mathbb E^0[(\mu-\delta_0)(\{0\})]=2\cdot1$. Thus $K(0)=1/2$; deleting both origin occurrences would incorrectly give zero.

The simple lattice has an atomic reduced measure and no pair-correlation density, while the doubled lattice verifies that factorial pairs distinguish occurrence indices and Palm deletion removes exactly one occurrence. The origin-centered convention and the closed-ball endpoint $r=0$ are both used explicitly. AC and Countable Choice [A1] are inherited assumptions only.

The density is unique up to Lebesgue-null sets. Normalize it by $\rho^2$ and call the resulting nonnegative Borel function $g$:

$$K(r):=\rho^{-1}\int(\mu-\delta_0)(B[0,r])\,P^0(d\mu),$$

For every Borel $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

Assume AC and Countable Choice as carried by the point-process supplier. For every stationary locally finite point process $\eta$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite positive intensity $\rho$, there is a unique probability law $P^0$ on the configuration space satisfying

$$\mathbb E\int h(x,\theta_x\eta)\,\eta(dx)=\rho\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int h(x,\mu)\,P^0(d\mu)\,dx$$

for every nonnegative product-measurable $h$. Moreover, $P^0$-almost every configuration has at least one occurrence at the origin.

Fix a locally compact, second-countable Hausdorff topological space $S$
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-second-countable-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Here locally compact means that every point has a
compact neighbourhood; second countable means that the topology has an at most
countable basis; and Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint open
neighbourhoods. Let $\mathcal B(S)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the
open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A **counting measure** on $S$ is a Borel measure of the form
$\mu=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{x_j}$ for a finite or countable index set $J$ and
points $x_j\in S$, where repetitions are allowed and the empty sum is zero.
Each $\delta_x$ is the unit point mass at $x$
([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), and
the countable sum is a measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]. The **multiplicity** at $x$ is
$\mu(\{x\})$. The counting measure is **locally finite** if
$\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact subset $K\subseteq S$
([[def-compact-space]]).

Let $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of locally finite counting
measures, equipped with the sigma-algebra generated by the **evaluation maps**
$\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(S)$. A **point process** on $S$ is a
measurable map $\eta:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to
(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$ from a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), with measurability in the sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Equivalently, every
count $\eta(B)$ is a measurable random variable, because the evaluation maps
generate $\mathcal E$. Its **law** is the probability measure
$\mathbb P_\eta(A)=\mathbb P(\eta^{-1}(A))$ on $(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]],
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]). The process is
classified by its realized configurations: a configuration $\mu$ is
**simple** if $\mu(\{x\})\le1$ for every $x$, and is **multiplicity-bearing**
if some singleton has mass greater than one. This is a pointwise distinction;
no almost-sure simplicity assertion is part of this definition.

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of all locally finite Borel
measures on $S$, with the sigma-algebra generated by their evaluation maps. A
**random locally finite measure** $\xi$ is a measurable map into this space.

For a nonnegative Borel function $f$, write
$\eta(f):=\int_S f\,d\eta$. Define the expected measure, or **intensity
measure**, by $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$. The expected-measure and
random-integral measurability assertions are justified by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]]. The measure
$\nu$ need not be locally finite; it is locally finite exactly when
$\mathbb E[\eta(K)]<\infty$ for each compact $K$.

The mean measure of a random locally finite measure is likewise
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, covered by the same expected-measure lemma. Local
finiteness of each realization does not by itself assert local finiteness of
$\nu$.

derivations.claim:
Apply [F2] with $D=B[0,r]$ and divide by $\rho^2>0$. By the K definition [F1],
$$K(r)=\rho^{-2}\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(B[0,r]).$$
The density clause in [F1] applied to the same closed ball gives $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(B[0,r])=\rho^2\int_{B[0,r]}g(u)du$. Substitution in step 1.1 proves the asserted integral formula.

Suppose $\eta$ is simple. The event $A_2=\{\mu:\mu(\{0\})\ge2\}$ is measurable by the evaluation sigma-algebra. In the refined Campbell identity [F3], take $h(x,\mu)=\mathbf1_Q(x)\mathbf1_{A_2}(\mu)$ with $Q=[0,1)^d$. On the probability-one event of simple realizations, every counted occurrence $x$ has $(\theta_x\eta)(\{0\})=\eta(\{x\})=1$, so the left side is zero. The right side is $\rho|Q|P^0(A_2)=\rho P^0(A_2)$, hence $P^0(A_2)=0$. Combining this with the at-least-one origin property in [F3] gives $\mu(\{0\})=1$ $P^0$-almost surely. Therefore $(\mu-\delta_0)(B[0,r])=\mu(B[0,r]\setminus\{0\})$ $P^0$-almost surely, and the definition [F1] gives the stated simple-process formula.

At the endpoint $r=0$, the closed-ball convention gives $B[0,0]=\{0\}$, so $K(0)=\rho^{-1}\mathbb E^0[\mu(\{0\})-1]$; this is $0$ for a simple process, while any other co-located occurrences contribute in the multiplicity-bearing case. The proof uses no density-existence claim beyond the stated hypothesis. AC and Countable Choice [A1]–[A2] are inherited supplier assumptions, not additional derivation steps.
